title: Philippine Immigration Detention: Pay Up, or Your Deportation Never Moves
dek: A Chinese surfer held for 41 days in the Philippines saw not a prison but a business with a price list: beds, boxed meals, phones, lawyer fees — everything bought with cash, and those who don't pay stay locked up for years, even decades.
why: StoryFM's Behind Bars series. Medium information density but solid detail. The first half is a personal ordeal; the second half — the gang economy inside the detention center, the ransom quotes from scam companies, the lawyers jacking up prices on the spot — is where the real value is.
who: Founders and going-global operators interested in the situation of overseas Chinese, the Philippine business environment, and the machinery of gray industry and immigration corruption.
skip: 6:29-9:14 surfing history and startup background, unrelated to the core mechanism.

points.h: The Immigration Bureau quoted 1.5 million pesos to walk free on the spot
points.body: The night Feili was arrested, immigration officers pulled him aside and whispered, ‘I can help you.’ After talking to a lawyer, the word came back: hand over 1.5 million pesos, about 160,000-170,000 RMB, and you can be released immediately, no problem at all. Of the 12 to 13 people arrested in the same batch, no one agreed to pay. Everyone thought it was impossible that such a thing could still exist in 2026, and wanted to resolve it through normal legal procedure. But the price of refusing was this: they were transferred from the holding cells of the General Santos police station to the Immigration Bureau detention center in Manila, where Feili ultimately spent 41 days.

points.h: When his phone was confiscated, the money in Gcash was transferred out
points.body: When Feili was detained his phone was taken, and they asked for his unlock code. He assumed it was normal procedure and gave it. His phone unlock code was the same as his Gcash payment password — the Philippine equivalent of Alipay. For the next four or five days he applied however he could and never got the phone back, until he kept pressing the Chinese consulate and his lawyer, and the phone was finally returned. When he turned it on, the interface had all switched to English, and the Gcash transfer records showed money had been sent out — but the night before he got the phone back, it had been transferred back in. There was only about 1,000 RMB in there. Feili says it isn't about how much money it was, but that someone had touched it while the phone wasn't in his hands. His read: many Chinese in Manila doing gray-industry scams who get arrested go through this same shakedown layer, but they don't dare go to the Chinese consulate, because their phones are full of criminal evidence.

points.h: The air conditioning and takeout the Immigration Bureau promised exist — in another form
points.body: For those unwilling to buy their own plane ticket to be transferred, the Immigration Bureau works on them in shifts, saying conditions at the Manila bureau are excellent: air conditioning, plenty of freedom, you can work out, play basketball, order takeout, use your phone. Feili says they weren't lying — there really is air conditioning, you really can order takeout, it's just another form, a completely different form. They arrived at the main bureau detention center after three in the morning. Getting out of the vehicle, what he saw was a square area, an outer layer of iron grating, a sheet-metal roof above, and all around it iron cages like dog kennels, with long communal sleeping platforms inside, hundreds of people. At three in the morning many weren't sleeping — bare-chested, in nothing but underwear, they clung to the iron cages watching the newcomers. Feili says he and the other foreigners didn't say a word for several minutes after getting out, then it hit them: the Immigration Bureau had lied to them.

points.h: The detention center is a business invested in by a Chinese boss
points.body: What Feili heard inside was that this Immigration Bureau detention center was invested in by a Chinese boss, in cooperation with the Immigration Bureau, and that the beds, toilets and other facilities were all newly built by that Chinese boss. Foreigners could just stay, but Chinese who came in had to pay. The lowest-tier communal platform bed was 10,000 pesos a month, about 1,100-1,200 RMB. Wealthy pan bosses and gambling kingpins could pay 50,000 pesos a month, over 6,000 RMB, for a so-called ‘air-conditioned room’ — actually the same bed, just wrapped in tin foil and wooden boards, with a foam box of ice beside it, a hole cut in the box, and an exhaust fan drawing the cold air into the bed. That is where the Immigration Bureau's earlier claim that ‘there's air conditioning inside’ came from.

points.h: Chinese gangs collect protection money: you want out without paying?
points.body: On Feili's first day inside, the head of the Chinese gang came to collect a ‘rumor fee,’ saying the facilities were all their investment and there was no way to stay for free. Feili said he had no money, that he was here to serve time, so how could he be expected to pay on top of that. The gang boss said in a threatening tone: you're already in here and you don't want to spend money, and you still think you're getting out? Feili learned that the place is run by gangs, and the Chinese gang monopolizes all food, clothing and daily life for Chinese — running a Chinese restaurant and a Chinese supermarket. The whole detention center holds about 200 people; when Feili went in it was the off season, and there were still over 100 Chinese, more than half of them gambling and gray industry. The Chinese gang's employees draw wages — the head chef 10,000 pesos a month, the kitchen helper 5,000 pesos — very low wages, but many people can't get out precisely because they have no money for a lawyer, so they can only work to earn.

points.h: A young man from Yunnan held over a year, his family thought he died in Southeast Asia
points.body: A young man from Yunnan asked Feili for help. Before the pandemic he'd been lured to the Philippines by a high-salary recruitment ad; the moment he landed his phone and passport were taken, and he was dragged into a compound to run telecom scams, where the supervisor shocked him with an electric baton every day his numbers were bad. After the company was busted he served a few months, then was transferred to the Immigration Bureau detention center. The normal deportation procedure is simple — a few departments sign off, you buy your own ticket, and you go — but the Immigration Bureau, in order to extract money, keeps you locked up a long time, and without paying, the procedure won't move. He'd already been held over a year, with not a cent, no phone, eating only prison food every day, unable to reach his family, who thought he had died in Southeast Asia. Feili helped him write a letter in Chinese and translated it into English, and through an introduction from a Japanese man got to see the warden, who had a guard bring Feili's phone so the young man could add his father on WeChat and send a selfie and a voice message. Afterwards the Immigration Bureau bought a basic phone specifically to solve this problem.

points.h: Scam company ransom: 3 million pesos per person
points.body: The only Chinese person Feili talked with at any length was from a scam company whose 70 or 80 people were surrounded by the Immigration Bureau together with the police and the NBI, three agencies. The first shakedown was the NBI and police locking each person in a toilet — because there are no cameras in the toilets — and taking every valuable on their bodies. The second was the Immigration Bureau negotiating with the company boss for ransoms, a different quote per person: 1 million, 2 million, 3 million pesos, depending on the mood of the person in charge. That company negotiated at 3 million pesos per person, over 300,000 RMB. The boss ultimately ransomed 30 people — exactly the 30 held on one floor — and the rest were promised food deliveries until they got out. This young man ran an operation targeting the Japanese market, scamming middle-aged Japanese women; in his best month he made 2 million RMB, and bought a house and a car in his home county. Later he was kidnapped by a friend, had several hundred thousand transferred away, and was hit with a trumped-up illegal firearms charge by a dirty cop, so he couldn't leave.

points.h: The Philippine lawyer raised his price on the spot when he saw a Chinese client
points.body: In Cebu, Feili was introduced by a Lithuanian to a Philippine lawyer, quoted at 200,000 pesos, over 20,000 RMB, done in four weeks. After Feili got to Manila the lawyer came to visit, saw he was Chinese, and immediately raised the price, saying the earlier figure was the old price and the new price required another 120,000 pesos, over 10,000 RMB. Feili decided not to use him and wrote off the deposit, turning instead to a Chinese middleman. The Chinese middleman quoted over 30,000 RMB, four to six weeks, no more than six. Feili says the truly reliable Chinese middlemen know this procedure inside out, because everyone locked up in there is Chinese. In the end he was held inside for over 30 days, 41 days counting Cebu. The Lithuanian who introduced the Philippine lawyer still hadn't gotten out when Feili sent him a message.

Look at his corrupt bureaucratic system and its people separately. I still believe Filipinos are, by nature, very good people. But the bureaucratic system is truly too corrupt — the kind of bureaucratic system that drinks blood, human blood.
